title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
Content addressing makes objects immutable, integrity checkable and deduplicated, which publications (ADR-0019) need for manifests and the player's shared-file accounting (AT-05). Publishing by rename under the object lock gives a simple crash rule: a file may exist without a reference and is swept, but a reference never exists without its file. Per-company naming keeps tenants independent at the cost of storing a file twice when two companies upload it.
FFmpeg is the established tool for both inspection and conversion of every format the release needs, including EXIF orientation and metadata removal for images, so one external tool covers both kinds instead of FFmpeg plus an in-process image library. Running it as a separate executable keeps memory-safety defects in parsers out of the API process and lets timeouts and limits kill a hostile file. It also keeps Teluni's Apache-2.0 code separate from FFmpeg's GPL build. The trade-off is CPU-heavy work on the API host and a binary dependency that every environment must provide.

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: Alternatives Considered
text: Alternatives Considered

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: S3-compatible object storage now
text:
S3-compatible object storage now
A MinIO or cloud bucket would separate storage from the API host and scale later, but it adds a service to run on the single-host pilot or a paid dependency. The object interface keeps this as a later implementation without changing object identity.

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: Media in PostgreSQL
text:
Media in PostgreSQL
Large objects or `bytea` would make storage transactional, but they inflate database backups and I/O with gigabytes of video and complicate streaming and range reads.

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: libvips (sharp) for images and FFmpeg for video
text:
libvips (`sharp`) for images and FFmpeg for video
Faster image handling, but it parses untrusted images inside the API process and adds a second native toolchain to qualify and isolate.

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: A separate processing service with a broker
text:
A separate processing service with a broker
Stronger isolation and independent scaling, but it adds deployment and failure modes that the pilot does not yet need. A separate, network-less processing container running the same commands is the deployment-level hardening step, without changing this decision.

heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
Immutable, verifiable objects that publications and players can reference by hash.
Crash-safe publication and reference-safe purge with a single lock order.
Hostile files cannot run code in, or exhaust, the API process.

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
Conversion competes with the API for CPU on the pilot host; concurrency is limited to one job by default and long videos take minutes.
Every environment (development, CI, production image) must provide a compatible FFmpeg build, and its security updates become an operational duty.
Storage is tied to one host until another object store implementation exists; backups must cover the media volume together with PostgreSQL.

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
Backups and restore must copy the media volume and the database consistently; restored objects are verified against their hashes, and a sweep removes files without rows.
Moving to another object store copies objects by hash and switches the implementation; asset and object identities stay the same.
The production image must ship FFmpeg with its license notices (PJ-13).

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
text:
ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-19
**Acceptance scope:** The owner explicitly approved this decision and the eleven decisions of the programming design on 2026-10-19 under PH-24. Acceptance establishes the direction for local and CI implementation of PJ-10, not the player's evaluator (PJ-12) or device qualification (PH-08).

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Context
text:
Context
Teluni schedules playlists by local business time per screen: weekdays, local hours, overnight windows, inclusive final dates and all-day windows, interpreted in the screen's time zone or its branch's, never the server's (FR-06). The [release policies](../project/release-policies.md#time-and-scheduling) fix how DST gaps and repeated hours resolve and require the backend preview and the Android player to share fixtures. Node.js 24, the API runtime, does not ship the ECMAScript Temporal API, and the standard `Date` and `Intl` objects give offsets for an instant but no way to resolve a local time that falls in a gap or a repeated hour. D-10 has not selected a time-zone library.
This record decides how the API represents and resolves local time for schedules and how the API and the player agree on the results. The rules themselves are in the [programming design](../project/programming-design.md).

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
Teluni will evaluate schedules with a pure evaluator over the Temporal API and verify every implementation against one fixture file:
The API's programming module owns a pure TypeScript evaluator that takes rules, a default, an IANA zone name and an instant range and returns resolved segments. It never reads a clock or the process time zone.
Local dates and times are Temporal `PlainDate` and `PlainTime` values, instants are Temporal `Instant` values, and zone resolution uses `ZonedDateTime` with explicit disambiguation plus transition lookup for gaps. Until Node.js provides Temporal natively, the API uses the `temporal-polyfill` package, pinned to an exact version, imported only by the programming module.
Canonical fixtures in JSON (rules, zone, range and expected segments in UTC and local form, and expected validation codes) are owned by the API module and run by its tests. The player runs the same file against its implementation in PJ-12; neither implementation is the reference for the other.
Preview is computed only by the API; the panel displays its segments.

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
Temporal models exactly the concepts the policies use (plain local dates and times, instants, zones and explicit disambiguation), and its model matches `java.time`, which an Android player is expected to use, so both implementations reason in the same terms and the fixtures express the same cases. A spec-conformant polyfill keeps the code on the standard API, so removing it when Node.js ships Temporal is an import change rather than a rewrite. Fixtures, not shared code, are the contract between two runtimes in different languages. Keeping the evaluator pure makes validation, preview and tests deterministic and independent of the host.

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Alternatives Considered
text: Alternatives Considered

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Luxon or date-fns-tz
text:
Luxon or date-fns-tz
Mature libraries, but each has its own model of gaps and repeated hours that differs from `java.time` and from the standard on the way to Node.js, so the fixtures would encode library behavior rather than the policy.

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Hand-written resolution over Intl.DateTimeFormat
text:
Hand-written resolution over `Intl.DateTimeFormat`
Avoids a dependency, but searching transitions and disambiguating local times is where subtle errors appear, and the code would duplicate a standard that is about to ship.

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: A shared evaluator package compiled for both runtimes
text:
A shared evaluator package compiled for both runtimes
One implementation for the API and the player would remove the second implementation, but the player is a native Android application; embedding a JavaScript engine to run schedules adds a runtime and its own failure modes on the device.

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
Deterministic, host-independent schedule results with the selected DST rules.
One fixture file that both the API and the player must pass.
A direct path to native Temporal.

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
A runtime dependency in the API until Node.js ships Temporal, which must be kept current with the zone database it relies on (the polyfill uses the runtime's `Intl` zone data).
Two implementations of the evaluator, kept equal only by the fixtures.

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
Zone data comes from the Node.js runtime's ICU; updating Node.js updates zone rules, and preview results for future dates can change after a zone-database update, as on the device.
Replacing the polyfill with native Temporal removes the dependency and its import; the fixtures must still pass.

title: ADR-0030: Synchronize Screens by Polling with Signed Authorization Statements
heading: ADR-0030: Synchronize Screens by Polling with Signed Authorization Statements
text:
ADR-0030: Synchronize Screens by Polling with Signed Authorization Statements
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-20
**Acceptance scope:** The owner explicitly approved this decision and the ten decisions of the publication and synchronization design on 2026-10-20 under PH-25. Acceptance establishes the direction for local and CI implementation of PJ-11, not the player's conformance (PJ-12), hardware qualification (PH-08) or the provisioning of signing keys in a real environment (PJ-13).

title: ADR-0030: Synchronize Screens by Polling with Signed Authorization Statements
heading: Context
text:
Context
ADR-0019 adopted immutable publications and atomic player activation but selected no transport, manifest serialization, integrity metadata or cryptographic mechanism. The policies require that a screen detect a new desired publication within 30 seconds (AT-11), report its state every 30 seconds (AT-24), never be rolled back by stale or reordered messages, keep playing valid content offline for at most seven days after its last renewal (AT-15) and suspend time-dependent output when its clock cannot be trusted (AT-16). Screens authenticate with a device-generated bearer credential under ADR-0027, and the device enrollment design left a tamper-evident form of the offline deadline to this decision. The pilot runs one API process on one host (ADR-0021).
This record decides how screens learn their desired publication, how they obtain and verify its manifest and media, and how the server states, verifiably, what a screen may play and until when. The details are in the [publication and synchronization design](../project/publication-sync-design.md).

title: ADR-0030: Synchronize Screens by Polling with Signed Authorization Statements
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
Screens **poll**. Every 30 seconds a screen calls `POST /device/sync` with its state report and receives its status, time zone, desired publication and a new authorization statement. The server computes the desired publication from current rows at each call; it keeps no push channel and no per-screen delivery queue.
A publication's **manifest** is UTF-8 JSON produced in a fixed key order, stored as exact bytes and identified by their SHA-256. Media are delivered as display renditions identified by SHA-256. Manifests and media are downloadable only for the screen's current desired publication; superseded work coalesces by synchronizing again.
Each sync response carries an **authorization statement**: a compact JWS signed with ECDSA P-256 and SHA-256 (`ES256`) by the first key of a configured key ring. It names the screen and company, the server time of issue, an expiry seven days later and the publications (ID and manifest SHA-256) the screen may activate or keep active until then. The key set's public halves are served to screens, which pin them after pairing.
Manifests and exchanges carry a **protocol** number; the server answers with the highest protocol both sides support and serializes publications in the current and previous protocol for at least 90 days after a new one (AT-26).

title: ADR-0030: Synchronize Screens by Polling with Signed Authorization Statements
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
Polling at 30 seconds meets AT-11 and doubles as the AT-24 heartbeat with one request per screen, uses only the HTTPS path the device credential already protects, and survives proxies, restarts and the single-host deployment without connection state. Deriving desired state from authoritative rows makes ordering a property of the database rather than of message delivery, so no acknowledgement or crash can roll a screen back or lose an assignment. Exact stored bytes give the manifest an identity that a statement can sign; a structure regenerated or normalized on each request could not. A per-screen statement binds entitlement, expiry and a signed server time in one object the player can check offline and store next to its active generation, which makes the seven-day deadline and the choice of content tamper-evident on the device and gives the trusted clock a server reference. ECDSA P-256 is implemented by Node.js and by Android's standard security providers, so neither side needs a new cryptographic dependency.

title: ADR-0030: Synchronize Screens by Polling with Signed Authorization Statements
heading: Alternatives Considered
text: Alternatives Considered

title: ADR-0030: Synchronize Screens by Polling with Signed Authorization Statements
heading: Push through WebSocket, server-sent events or a broker
text:
Push through WebSocket, server-sent events or a broker
Detection within seconds, but AT-11 allows 30, and a persistent channel adds connection management, proxy configuration and reconnection on the pilot host. A push hint can be added later without changing the state model.

title: ADR-0030: Synchronize Screens by Polling with Signed Authorization Statements
heading: Fan-out of desired state into per-screen rows
text:
Fan-out of desired state into per-screen rows
Simple reads, but a crash between a publication and its fan-out needs a durable queue, and fan-out races with concurrent assignments. Computing from authoritative rows is always consistent and costs one indexed query per poll.

title: ADR-0030: Synchronize Screens by Polling with Signed Authorization Statements
heading: TLS only, without signed statements
text:
TLS only, without signed statements
TLS authenticates the server during transfer but leaves the stored deadline and content choice as plain local files. It also gives the player no signed time reference.

title: ADR-0030: Synchronize Screens by Polling with Signed Authorization Statements
heading: Signing manifests at publication
text:
Signing manifests at publication
Authenticates content once, but not which screen may play it or until when; a statement per screen covers both.

title: ADR-0030: Synchronize Screens by Polling with Signed Authorization Statements
heading: Ed25519 or a shared HMAC key
text:
Ed25519 or a shared HMAC key
Ed25519 is compact but not provided by older Android versions without an added library; an HMAC would require a secret on every screen, so any one screen could forge statements.

title: ADR-0030: Synchronize Screens by Polling with Signed Authorization Statements
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0030: Synchronize Screens by Polling with Signed Authorization Statements
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
Screens converge on the latest authorized publication within one polling interval, with no message ordering assumptions.
The player can verify offline which content it may show and until when, and anchor its clock to a signed server time.
No new infrastructure or cryptographic dependency on either side.

title: ADR-0030: Synchronize Screens by Polling with Signed Authorization Statements
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
Every screen makes a request every 30 seconds whether or not anything changed; the reference load of 100 screens is about 3.3 requests per second.
The signing key ring is a new production secret with rotation duties.
Detection is bounded by the polling interval, not immediate.

title: ADR-0030: Synchronize Screens by Polling with Signed Authorization Statements
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
`TELUNI_SYNC_SIGNING_KEYS` must be provisioned and backed up with the other secrets (PJ-13). Rotation adds a key at the front and keeps the previous one for at least seven days.
Restoring a database backup restores publications and desired state together; screens reconcile at their next poll. Pointing screens at a different host needs the same signing keys or a published key transition.
A future protocol needs dual serialization for the support window.

title: ADR-0031: Build the Player on a Portable Core with File-Based Atomic State and Managed Installation
heading: ADR-0031: Build the Player on a Portable Core with File-Based Atomic State and Managed Installation
text:
ADR-0031: Build the Player on a Portable Core with File-Based Atomic State and Managed Installation
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-20
**Acceptance scope:** The owner delegated every pending decision to the agent on 2026-10-20 (recorded with PH-25). The agent accepted this decision under that delegation together with the decisions of the [player design](../project/player-design.md); merging the pull request that adds it is the repository review. Acceptance establishes the direction for implementing PJ-12 in local and CI environments. It does not qualify any device (PH-08), select production update operations (PJ-13) or provide the release signing key (PH-27).

title: ADR-0031: Build the Player on a Portable Core with File-Based Atomic State and Managed Installation
heading: Context
text:
Context
ADR-0020 chose a native Kotlin and Media3 Android TV player with durable local state. It left the persistence library, startup and unattended behavior, packaging and updates open, and ADR-0019 requires atomic activation that survives power loss. The protocol of ADR-0030 gives screens exact manifests, SHA-256-identified media and signed statements with a server time, but says nothing about how the player stores them or how it gets reliable local time.
The pilot hardware is unknown (PH-08) and likely to include inexpensive Android TV boxes. Such boxes often run old Android versions with stale time zone data, have no battery-backed clock and offer limited launcher control. The repository's tooling is TypeScript, while the shared schedule fixtures must also run against the player. The cloud development environment cannot currently reach Google's Maven repository (PH-26).

title: ADR-0031: Build the Player on a Portable Core with File-Based Atomic State and Managed Installation
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
The player is one Gradle build in `apps/player`. A pure-JVM `core` module holds every rule: protocol models, statement verification, the schedule evaluator, trusted time, the local store, synchronization and playback decisions. An Android `app` module holds the activity, Media3 rendering, the Keystore vault and device integration. `core` tests run the repository's shared fixtures, and a dedicated CI job checks the build as part of the required gate.
Local state is plain files in app-private storage, without a database:
write-once media named by their SHA-256;
exact manifest bytes per generation;
one small state record replaced atomically (temporary file, `fsync`, rename, directory `fsync`).
Activation is a single replacement of that record, and startup reconciles deterministically from any interruption.
Business time never depends on the device's time zone data. Each sync response carries the screen zone's UTC offsets for the next 35 days, computed by the API with the same Temporal implementation as the preview. Trusted time comes from a monotonic anchor set at each sync, with a persisted lower bound across reboots.
The supported unattended profile makes the player the device owner on a reset device: the HOME activity in lock task mode. Updates are APKs that the API distributes, verified by SHA-256 and signing certificate and installed by the device owner inside a local window. The player never downgrades; a rollback is a roll-forward release.

title: ADR-0031: Build the Player on a Portable Core with File-Based Atomic State and Managed Installation
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
Keeping rules in a JVM module lets the evaluator, protocol parsing, cryptographic checks and store faults be tested quickly and exhaustively in CI without emulators. The same code runs on the device. It also lets that work proceed while Android tooling is unavailable in some environments.
The persistent state is a handful of pointers plus immutable files. Atomic file replacement has a simple failure model that can be fault-injected at every step. A database would add schema migrations that interact badly with the no-downgrade rule. Its own durability under power loss would still need the same testing.
Server-supplied offsets remove a real failure mode: a pilot box with pre-2019 time zone data would shift `America/Sao_Paulo` schedules by an hour for months. They also make the player agree with the server's preview by construction. The cost is a small additive field in the sync response and evaluation that stops outside the covered range, which the seven-day authorization already bounds.
On Android 10 and later, a background `BOOT_COMPLETED` start is unreliable, and an ordinary app cannot update itself without a prompt. Device-owner mode makes boot, crash recovery and scheduled updates work without a person at the screen. In exchange, an installer must provision each device with `adb` after a reset, which is acceptable for a pilot of a few screens.
These are reasoned choices, not measurements. Startup, recovery, clock behavior and power-loss safety still need PH-08 hardware evidence.

title: ADR-0031: Build the Player on a Portable Core with File-Based Atomic State and Managed Installation
heading: Alternatives Considered
text: Alternatives Considered

title: ADR-0031: Build the Player on a Portable Core with File-Based Atomic State and Managed Installation
heading: Room or another embedded database
text:
Room or another embedded database
Offers queries and transactional updates, but adds migrations, a larger failure surface and the same need for power-cut evidence. Nothing in the state needs relational queries.

title: ADR-0031: Build the Player on a Portable Core with File-Based Atomic State and Managed Installation
heading: Device or bundled time zone data
text:
Device or bundled time zone data
Device data can be years out of date on unmanaged boxes. A bundled library (ThreeTenBP or Joda-Time) is updated only with player releases and can still disagree with the server preview.

title: ADR-0031: Build the Player on a Portable Core with File-Based Atomic State and Managed Installation
heading: Basic installation with Google Play updates
text:
Basic installation with Google Play updates
Store distribution needs accounts, review and Play on every device. It does not install updates unattended inside a business window, and many commercial boxes lack Play. A basic sideloaded profile stays possible where PH-08 shows that it boots and recovers reliably.

title: ADR-0031: Build the Player on a Portable Core with File-Based Atomic State and Managed Installation
heading: A single Android module
text:
A single Android module
Simpler build files, but every rule test would need Robolectric or an emulator, and no part could be built without the Android SDK.

title: ADR-0031: Build the Player on a Portable Core with File-Based Atomic State and Managed Installation
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0031: Build the Player on a Portable Core with File-Based Atomic State and Managed Installation
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
Rules, protocol conformance and crash recovery are tested on every pull request with the shared fixtures and the API's conformance fixtures.
Schedules agree with the preview regardless of the device's time zone data.
Managed devices boot into content, recover from crashes and update unattended.

title: ADR-0031: Build the Player on a Portable Core with File-Based Atomic State and Managed Installation
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
The repository gains a second build system and a JVM toolchain, with its own dependency verification and Renovate coverage.
Managed installation requires `adb` provisioning on a factory-reset device and excludes devices that cannot be made device owner from the supported profile.
Without a server answer after a reboot, the player depends on the system clock being at least the persisted bound and set by network time; a wrong clock without a reference cannot always be detected.
The API must keep serving zone offsets and conformance fixtures as part of the device contract.

title: ADR-0031: Build the Player on a Portable Core with File-Based Atomic State and Managed Installation
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
Release signing needs a human-held key (PH-27), and production releases need an approval and update-window process (PJ-13).
Changing the local state format requires a forward migration or a re-synchronization that keeps the credential. Rollbacks are new releases.
Building the Android module in the current cloud environment requires allowing Google's Maven host (PH-26).

title: ADR-0032: Represent Money as Integer Minor Units with a Currency per Field
heading: ADR-0032: Represent Money as Integer Minor Units with a Currency per Field
text:
ADR-0032: Represent Money as Integer Minor Units with a Currency per Field
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-20
**Acceptance scope:** The owner delegated every pending decision to the agent on 2026-10-20 (recorded with PH-25). The agent accepted this decision under that delegation together with the [catalog and composition design](../project/catalog-composition-design.md); merging the pull request that adds it is the repository review. It settles the monetary representation that D-10 left open for catalogs, prices, publications and the player. It does not select a currency conversion service, because the policies forbid conversion.

title: ADR-0032: Represent Money as Integer Minor Units with a Currency per Field
heading: Context

title: ADR-0032: Represent Money as Integer Minor Units with a Currency per Field
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
An amount is an integer count of the currency's minor units: `1990` BRL is R$ 19,90, and `1990` JPY is ¥1,990. It is stored as PostgreSQL `bigint` and transported in JSON as an integer within ±(2^53 − 1) and in practice far below. The API refuses values outside 0 to 10^12 minor units.
The currency is an ISO 4217 alphabetic code fixed on the money field when the field is created. Every value, override and promotion of that field uses it. A field's currency never changes; changing currency means adding a field.
The number of minor units comes from a table in the API, checked against `Intl.NumberFormat` in tests and copied to the player. The input `"19,9"` in `pt-BR` or `"19.90"` in `en-US` is parsed by the panel into minor units, rejecting more decimals than the currency has.
Formatting for people uses the locale, through `Intl.NumberFormat` in the web panel and `java.text.NumberFormat`/`Currency` on the player, with the field's currency. Locale never changes the amount or the currency. Amounts are never converted between currencies.
Non-monetary decimals (`number` fields) are canonical decimal strings with a fixed number of places, never floats.

title: ADR-0032: Represent Money as Integer Minor Units with a Currency per Field
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
Integer minor units are exact, compare and sort trivially, and mean the same in SQL, JSON, TypeScript and Kotlin without a decimal library.
A currency per field rules out mixing currencies inside one price list by construction. That is the common case for a business operating in one country, and the policies forbid conversion anyway.
The cost is that a business pricing the same product in two currencies needs two fields, which is honest about the meaning.

title: ADR-0032: Represent Money as Integer Minor Units with a Currency per Field
heading: Alternatives Considered
text: Alternatives Considered

title: ADR-0032: Represent Money as Integer Minor Units with a Currency per Field
heading: PostgreSQL numeric and decimal strings everywhere
text:
PostgreSQL numeric and decimal strings everywhere
Exact, but every runtime then needs a decimal implementation and a rule for scale. A value like `19.9` versus `19.90` invites accidental inequality. Minor units carry the scale in the currency.

title: ADR-0032: Represent Money as Integer Minor Units with a Currency per Field
heading: A currency on each value
text:
A currency on each value
More flexible, but it allows a price list in mixed currencies that cannot be compared or validated, and nothing in the product needs it.

title: ADR-0033: Expose the Pilot Host with End-to-End TLS and Back It Up with Encrypted Off-Host Snapshots
heading: ADR-0033: Expose the Pilot Host with End-to-End TLS and Back It Up with Encrypted Off-Host Snapshots
text:
ADR-0033: Expose the Pilot Host with End-to-End TLS and Back It Up with Encrypted Off-Host Snapshots
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-22
**Acceptance scope:** On 2026-10-22 the owner asked the agent to take every pending decision that is only a decision, which extends the delegation recorded with PH-25. The agent accepted this decision under that delegation together with the decisions of the [deployment design](../project/deployment-design.md); merging the pull request that adds it is the repository review. Acceptance establishes the direction for building and rehearsing the deployment in PJ-13. It does not verify the owner's host or network (PH-10), create any account, or authorize exposing a host.

title: ADR-0033: Expose the Pilot Host with End-to-End TLS and Back It Up with Encrypted Off-Host Snapshots
heading: Context
text:
Context
ADR-0021 chose a single residential Debian host with Docker Compose, a reverse proxy with HTTPS and durable local media. It deliberately selected no tunnel, proxy, object store or provider, and it made real-customer use conditional on off-host recovery and owner-approved recovery targets. Residential lines in Brazil are often behind CGNAT or block inbound ports, and the owner has no recurring cloud budget.
Screens download video renditions, and people upload videos of up to 1 GiB in a single request. Sessions are server-managed cookies, and media are private to their company. Screens play for up to seven days without the server (AT-15), which bounds how long a recovery can take.

title: ADR-0033: Expose the Pilot Host with End-to-End TLS and Back It Up with Encrypted Off-Host Snapshots
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
TLS ends on the owner's host, in a Caddy reverse proxy that obtains Let's Encrypt certificates. The host is reached directly when the line has a usable public address. Otherwise it is reached through a TCP relay on a free-tier virtual machine that forwards encrypted traffic through a WireGuard tunnel opened by the host. No TLS-terminating tunnel, CDN or proxy service sits in front of Teluni.
Backups are restic snapshots, encrypted on the host, of the PostgreSQL dumps followed by hard links of the content-addressed media objects, taken under a lock that keeps object files from being deleted in between. They are written every 6 hours to an S3-compatible bucket at a separate provider, initially Backblaze B2, and kept for at most about 35 days. Secrets are excluded from snapshots and kept offline by the owner.

title: ADR-0033: Expose the Pilot Host with End-to-End TLS and Back It Up with Encrypted Off-Host Snapshots
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
Ending TLS on the host keeps session cookies, credentials and private media away from intermediaries. The relay is replaceable and holds nothing.
A TLS-terminating free tunnel would solve CGNAT, but its terms restrict serving video outside paid products. Its reported upload cap is below the media limit, and it would see every session.
Object files are written before the rows that record them and deleted only after those rows, under an advisory lock that the backup holds from before its dumps until it has hard-linked the objects. That makes "dumps first, then objects" a consistent set without stopping the service or making anyone wait on the upload. The restore check verifies it.
Client-side encryption lets a free off-host bucket hold customer data as ciphertext only. Deduplication keeps 6-hourly snapshots within the free allowance at pilot scale.
A 6-hour recovery point and a 72-hour worst-case recovery time keep screens playing through any recovery under AT-15.
Assumptions: provider allowances (Oracle Cloud's outbound transfer, Backblaze B2's free storage and downloads) are as reported in October 2026. They can change, so the destination and relay must stay replaceable. Whether the owner's line needs the relay is unknown until PH-10.

title: ADR-0033: Expose the Pilot Host with End-to-End TLS and Back It Up with Encrypted Off-Host Snapshots
heading: Alternatives Considered
text: Alternatives Considered

title: ADR-0033: Expose the Pilot Host with End-to-End TLS and Back It Up with Encrypted Off-Host Snapshots
heading: A TLS-terminating tunnel (Cloudflare Tunnel or similar)
text:
A TLS-terminating tunnel (Cloudflare Tunnel or similar)
Free, and it avoids port forwarding, but it ends TLS at the provider. It conflicts with the CDN terms for video, and its reported 100 MB upload cap rejects valid uploads. Rejected for this service.

title: ADR-0033: Expose the Pilot Host with End-to-End TLS and Back It Up with Encrypted Off-Host Snapshots
heading: Running everything on the free-tier virtual machine
text:
Running everything on the free-tier virtual machine
Removes the residential risks at no cost. It would, however, put customer data under the provider's idle-reclamation and account terms with no paid support. It is kept only as a relay.

title: ADR-0033: Expose the Pilot Host with End-to-End TLS and Back It Up with Encrypted Off-Host Snapshots
heading: Continuous WAL archiving
text:
Continuous WAL archiving
Reduces the recovery point to minutes, at the cost of a second backup and restore mechanism. Deferred until a customer needs a smaller recovery point.

heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0033: Expose the Pilot Host with End-to-End TLS and Back It Up with Encrypted Off-Host Snapshots
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
No intermediary sees decrypted traffic or backups.
No recurring cost at pilot scale, and every external piece (relay, bucket, mail relay) can be replaced without changing the application.
Deleted data leaves backups within about 35 days, which the data handling policies can state.

title: ADR-0033: Expose the Pilot Host with End-to-End TLS and Back It Up with Encrypted Off-Host Snapshots
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
The owner operates certificates, the relay and backup monitoring. A failed backup is only noticed through the alerts the deployment design requires.
Losing the offline restic password loses every backup. Losing the secret key rings after a restore invalidates sessions and sealed mail credentials.
Free tiers can change their terms. The design names fallbacks, but switching still takes work.

text:
Operational or Migration Impact
PJ-13 builds the Compose bundle, the backup, restore and verification scripts, and a rehearsal that CI runs. The real-host rehearsal and runbooks wait for PH-10. Moving to a paid VPS later keeps the same composition, with the relay removed.

title: ADR-0034: Build Data Grids on TanStack Table and TanStack Virtual
heading: ADR-0034: Build Data Grids on TanStack Table and TanStack Virtual
text:
ADR-0034: Build Data Grids on TanStack Table and TanStack Virtual
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-27
**Acceptance scope:** On 2026-10-27 the owner asked for sorting, column filters, column resizing and configurable multiple selection in the shared `DataSet`, designed for very many rows, and asked the agent to use the best available technology. The agent accepted this decision under that request and the delegation recorded with [PH-25](../project/human-actions.md#ph-25); merging the pull request that adds it is the repository review. It selects the web panel's grid libraries. It does not add server-side sorting or filtering to any API.

title: ADR-0034: Build Data Grids on TanStack Table and TanStack Virtual
heading: Context

title: ADR-0034: Build Data Grids on TanStack Table and TanStack Virtual
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
The web panel builds grids on two headless libraries, pinned exactly in `apps/web`:
**TanStack Table v9** (`@tanstack/react-table`) owns the grid model: sorting, column filtering, value faceting and column sizing/resizing, with only those features registered.
**TanStack Virtual v3** (`@tanstack/react-virtual`) renders only the rows, and filter options, in view.
Teluni renders all markup itself in the shared `DataGrid`, which `DataSet` composes, and the shared `MultiSelectList`. Row selection remains caller-owned rather than table state, so features keep selection next to their URL and API state. Sorting and filtering run in the browser over the rows the caller supplies; a list that cannot load all its rows needs server-side sorting and filtering added to its API first.

title: ADR-0034: Build Data Grids on TanStack Table and TanStack Virtual
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
Both libraries are headless, so the product keeps its semantic markup, ARIA grid roles, keyboard model and token-based styling.
They belong to the TanStack family already selected by ADR-0008, are MIT-licensed and widely used, and add only the registered features to the bundle.
TanStack Table's faceting gives each column's distinct values while applying the other columns' filters, which is the behavior a value filter needs. Its row models are memoized and recompute only when data or state change.
Virtualization keeps the DOM to a few dozen rows regardless of size. In a development build, 10,000 rows sorted in about 75 ms and a filter with 10,000 distinct values opened in about 80 ms rendering 14 options.
TanStack Table v9's React adapter returns a new table reference when its state changes, so components compiled by the React Compiler update. The virtualizer keeps one instance whose output changes while scrolling, so the components that read it opt out with the `"use no memo"` directive.

title: ADR-0034: Build Data Grids on TanStack Table and TanStack Virtual
heading: Alternatives Considered
text: Alternatives Considered

title: ADR-0034: Build Data Grids on TanStack Table and TanStack Virtual
heading: A complete data grid component (for example AG Grid or MUI X Data Grid)
text:
A complete data grid component (for example AG Grid or MUI X Data Grid)
These provide sorting, filtering and virtualization, but bring their own markup, styling system and theming, are much larger, and reserve some features for commercial licenses. Adapting them to the product's tokens and accessibility choices would fight the library.

title: ADR-0034: Build Data Grids on TanStack Table and TanStack Virtual
heading: Own implementation without libraries
text:
Own implementation without libraries
Sorting and selection are small, but virtualization with scrolling to a row, faceting under interacting filters and live column resizing would be new code with its own defects and tests, duplicating mature libraries.

title: ADR-0034: Build Data Grids on TanStack Table and TanStack Virtual
heading: Virtualization only, with an own grid model
text:
Virtualization only, with an own grid model
TanStack Virtual alone solves rendering size, but leaves the faceting and resizing edge cases above to the product.

title: ADR-0034: Build Data Grids on TanStack Table and TanStack Virtual
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0034: Build Data Grids on TanStack Table and TanStack Virtual
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
One grid serves small lists like companies and large in-browser lists, with consistent sorting, filtering, resizing and selection.
The headless model keeps the existing styling, theme and accessibility responsibilities in the product.

title: ADR-0034: Build Data Grids on TanStack Table and TanStack Virtual
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
Two runtime dependencies to keep current; TanStack Table v9 is recent, so upgrades need the browser tests that cover the grid.
Sorting and filtering apply only to loaded rows; paginated lists filter the loaded page until their APIs support server-side processing.
Text sorts with `Intl.Collator` for the person's locale without numeric collation, which was about 2.7 times slower in measurement; "Loja 10" therefore sorts before "Loja 9". Numeric values sort as numbers.

heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
No API, database or deployment change. Replacing either library would affect only `apps/web/src/data-grid.tsx` and `apps/web/src/multi-select-list.tsx`.

title: ADR-0035: Export Grid Data in the Browser to XLSX, CSV and PDF
heading: ADR-0035: Export Grid Data in the Browser to XLSX, CSV and PDF
text:
ADR-0035: Export Grid Data in the Browser to XLSX, CSV and PDF
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-27
**Acceptance scope:** On 2026-10-27 the owner asked for exports of the data the shared `DataSet` shows, at least to Excel and PDF, and left further formats and the technology to the agent. The agent accepted this decision under that request and the delegation recorded with [PH-25](../project/human-actions.md#ph-25); merging the pull request that adds it is the repository review. It covers exports of rows the browser already shows. It adds no export endpoint or server-side report.

title: ADR-0035: Export Grid Data in the Browser to XLSX, CSV and PDF
heading: Context
text:
Context
[ADR-0034](0034-build-data-grids-on-tanstack-table-and-tanstack-virtual.md) gives the web panel a grid that sorts and filters the rows it holds. People need to take that view elsewhere: analyze it in a spreadsheet, load it into another system, or print and share it. The rows are already authorized for the person and present in the browser, and the grid can hold tens of thousands of them. Teluni's audience works mostly in Portuguese spreadsheets, which expect `;` separators and decimal commas in CSV. Export code must not slow the first page load.

title: ADR-0035: Export Grid Data in the Browser to XLSX, CSV and PDF
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
Grids offer three formats, opt-in per screen through `exportName`:
**Excel (.xlsx)** through `write-excel-file`, keeping numbers numeric, the header bold and frozen, and the column widths shown;
**CSV** generated by the product: UTF-8 with a byte order mark, CRLF lines, the locale's separator and decimal mark (`;` and `,` in Portuguese), and text that a spreadsheet would run as a formula prefixed with `'`;
**PDF** through `jsPDF` with `jspdf-autotable`: A4, landscape for wide grids, a title, the generation time and record count, and page numbers.
An export contains the rows the grid shows, in their order and with its filters, and the columns that have a value. It runs entirely in the browser.
The libraries are pinned exactly and loaded with dynamic `import()` only when someone exports.

title: ADR-0035: Export Grid Data in the Browser to XLSX, CSV and PDF
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
XLSX keeps types and opens directly in Excel, LibreOffice and Google Sheets; CSV is what other systems import; PDF is what people print, attach and sign off. A JSON export would serve developers rather than the panel's users and is left out.
`write-excel-file` is MIT-licensed, maintained, browser-first and depends only on `fflate`. The SheetJS package on the public registry stopped at 0.18.5 in 2022 with known advisories, and ExcelJS has not been released since 2023 and pulls Node-oriented dependencies.
`jsPDF` with `jspdf-autotable` is the established MIT pair for tables in the browser, paginates repeated headers and handles Portuguese accents with its built-in Helvetica (WinAnsi encoding).
Generating CSV needs no library; doing it in the product keeps the locale and formula-injection rules explicit and tested.
In a development build, 10,000 rows exported in about 0.1 s to CSV, 0.6 s to XLSX and 3 s to a 7 MB PDF.

title: ADR-0035: Export Grid Data in the Browser to XLSX, CSV and PDF
heading: Alternatives Considered
text: Alternatives Considered

title: ADR-0035: Export Grid Data in the Browser to XLSX, CSV and PDF
heading: Print the page to PDF
text:
Print the page to PDF
The browser's print dialog would need no library, but virtualization renders only the rows in view, and saving a PDF would depend on the person choosing a printer destination.

title: ADR-0035: Export Grid Data in the Browser to XLSX, CSV and PDF
heading: Server-side exports
text:
Server-side exports
An API export could cover more rows than the browser holds, but it needs endpoints, authorization and limits for each list. It remains possible for lists that add server-side sorting and filtering.

title: ADR-0035: Export Grid Data in the Browser to XLSX, CSV and PDF
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0035: Export Grid Data in the Browser to XLSX, CSV and PDF
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
Every screen with a grid can offer the same three exports by passing one prop; the first page load does not include the export libraries.

title: ADR-0035: Export Grid Data in the Browser to XLSX, CSV and PDF
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
Three runtime dependencies to keep current. jsPDF installs optional packages (html2canvas, DOMPurify, canvg, core-js) that the build emits as unused lazy chunks; core-js's install script stays disabled.
The PDF uses a standard font, so characters outside WinAnsi, such as emoji, do not print. Very large PDFs take seconds and many pages.
`fflate` compresses XLSX in a worker created from a `blob:` URL; a future Content Security Policy must allow `worker-src blob:`.

title: ADR-0035: Export Grid Data in the Browser to XLSX, CSV and PDF
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
Exports are files the person saves on their device; the product does not log or store them. A screen that must not let records leave the panel simply omits `exportName`.

title: ADR Instructions
heading: ADR Instructions
text:
ADR Instructions
Consult the [decision index](README.md) and [authoring policy](authoring.md) before creating or changing an ADR.
Start new proposals with the [template](template.md) and `proposed` status. Acceptance is distinct from implementation completion.
Preserve accepted rationale, decisions, dates, and stable identifiers. Architectural changes require a new decision and explicit supersession, not rewritten history.
Retain meaningful alternatives, negative consequences, constraints, and evidence. Do not invent evaluations to fill the template.
Update current policy and reciprocal supersession references when an accepted architectural change requires them.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
text:
Authoring Architecture Decision Records
Use the [decision index](README.md) to search existing decisions and the [template](template.md) to draft a record. ADRs preserve decision history and rationale; current policy describes current architecture. Git, migrations, changelogs, design documents, and runbooks retain their separate responsibilities.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: When a decision needs an ADR
text:
When a decision needs an ADR
Create an ADR for a significant choice whose rationale a future contributor cannot reliably infer from implementation. Relevant effects include system boundaries, dependency direction, ownership, runtime/deployment topology, security, persistence, public contracts, cross-cutting technology, operational behavior, and long-term maintainability.
Consider the breadth, reversibility, long-term dependency, plausible alternatives, integrity/security implications, and risk of losing the reasoning. Ordinary local refactors, fixes, tests, small helpers, individual indexes, and routine dependency additions do not each need an ADR. Major technology choices generally do. Existing foundation policies do not each need retroactive ADRs.
An ADR records a sufficiently concrete architectural conclusion, not every discussion or rejected idea. It must not become a task tracker, changelog, runbook, detailed implementation design, or snapshot of volatile vendor data. A separate RFC system is not required. Bundle decisions only when their rationale and lifecycle belong together; avoid giant records deciding unrelated parts of the stack.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Lifecycle and historical integrity
text:
Lifecycle and historical integrity
Status
Meaning
`proposed`
Under active consideration; implementation must not assume finality unless explicitly exploratory
`accepted`
Approved architectural direction; implementation and current documentation should align, allowing an explicit migration period
`rejected`
Considered and deliberately not adopted
`superseded`
Previously accepted, then replaced by another decision; link the replacement
`deprecated`
Historically relevant but no longer appropriate for new architecture; use sparingly when replacement is transitional or incomplete
Do not add statuses without a clear need. Normal transitions are proposed to accepted/rejected and accepted to superseded/deprecated. Do not normally revert historical decisions to proposed; create a new record when reconsidering them.
Accepted does not mean implemented or released. Track pending/partial/completed implementation through normal issues, tasks, or pull requests, not extra ADR statuses. Exploratory work and proofs of concept provide evidence but do not themselves establish acceptance. Long-lived production implementation should generally not rely on an unresolved major proposal.
Accepted substantive history should remain immutable. Non-semantic spelling, formatting, broken-link, and obvious-typo corrections may be acceptable, but must not change historical meaning. When architecture changes, create a new ADR. Retain the old record, mark it superseded, and add reciprocal `Supersedes` / `Superseded by` references. Keep the original date. For partial supersession, identify precisely what remains valid, what changed, and which decision replaces it.
Rejected records can preserve useful evaluation and constraints; a changed context can justify reconsideration in a new ADR. Do not treat rejection as a permanent prohibition. Purely local abandoned proposals may be removed before meaningful shared history; preserve broadly reviewed or referenced proposals as rejected where useful. Do not record every immediately dismissed idea.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Identity and metadata
text:
Identity and metadata
Use monotonic numeric identifiers and descriptive English filenames of the form `NNNN-short-decision-title.md`. Numbers identify records, not importance, domain, priority, or version. Gaps are acceptable. Never reuse or renumber identifiers already in shared history. Resolve parallel numbering conflicts before merge; an unshared identifier may be changed.
When a foundation upgrade brings an already published identifier that collides with a project decision, retain both records and their identifiers. Import the foundation record under `docs/adr/orion/`, with its own decision index and corrected relative links. Each directory is an identifier namespace; validation enforces unique IDs and index membership within each namespace and the same metadata requirements for every record. New Teluni decisions remain in `docs/adr/`; this exception preserves independent published histories rather than allocating new product namespaces.
Record title, status, date, context, decision, and consequences. For accepted records, the date should generally be the acceptance date. Titles should describe the decision rather than merely name a topic. Preserve identifiers once merged and referenced.
Simple Markdown metadata is the current format. `pnpm docs:check` validates filenames, matching titles/IDs, status, ISO dates, required sections, and index membership. Preserve these field names as tooling contracts. Supersession semantics still require review; no automatic numbering or supersession checker is implemented. ADR files remain canonical; avoid duplicate status stores or custom ADR software without a concrete need.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Content and evidence
text:
Content and evidence
**Context:** explain the actual problem, relevant constraints, scope, timing, and assumptions. Avoid unnecessary implementation detail.
**Decision:** state the chosen direction clearly enough to understand independently of the alternatives.
**Rationale:** explain the material tradeoffs, evidence, and constraints. Distinguish confirmed evidence, reasoned tradeoffs, and assumptions.
**Alternatives:** describe serious alternatives considered; do not fabricate alternatives or evaluation evidence to fill a template.
**Consequences:** include benefits, costs, limitations, new responsibilities, security/operational effects, and reversibility or migration costs where relevant. Formal scoring is not required.
**References:** link relevant repository policy, earlier decisions, designs, benchmarks, proofs of concept, and durable evidence. Avoid unnecessary dependency graphs and large volatile datasets. Preserve enough explanation that disappearing external links do not destroy the rationale.
Use current evidence at decision time when product capability, support lifecycle, pricing, security status, or provider limits matter. Vendor documentation can support constraints but must not be the sole location of the explanation. Detailed implementation and operational migration steps normally belong outside the ADR.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Creation, review, and acceptance
text:
Creation, review, and acceptance
Search the index and related policies for the same question, accepted direction, superseded decision, or rejected alternative. Determine whether this is an architectural decision rather than an implementation detail.
Allocate the next available identifier, copy the template, and use `proposed` status.
Document context, explicit direction, meaningful alternatives, rationale, constraints, and positive and negative consequences while the context is still known.
Review in proportion to impact: is the problem real, the complexity justified, and the choice consistent with existing architecture? Identify conflicts and intentional deviations explicitly.
Accept or reject through repository review. For a small team, review, merge, and accepted status are sufficient; do not add governance ceremony without a concrete need.
On acceptance, update affected current documentation and implement the selected direction with relevant verification. Do not retain rejected experimental paths unnecessarily.
For supersession, additionally identify changed constraints, reciprocal references, affected current policy, and compatibility/migration work. For rejection, record decisive reasons, preferred alternatives where applicable, and conditions that could justify reconsideration.
Retrospective ADRs should say the decision was already in effect. Record only known reasoning and state uncertainty rather than inventing a historical evaluation. Significant principle deviations belong in the decision and corresponding current-policy update. When later accepted decisions supersede older records, follow the replacement and current policy rather than treating the superseded record as current architecture.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Maintenance and deferred mechanisms
text:
Maintenance and deferred mechanisms
Routine maintenance should be limited to permitted corrections and supersession metadata. Current architecture must remain discoverable without reading the entire chronological ADR history. Keep descriptive titles, explicit technologies/concepts, and useful related references.
Frontmatter, automatic numbering, generated indexing, status/supersession validation, approval workflows, and required reviewers remain tooling or organizational decisions. Introduce them only when justified. ADRs should preserve meaningful reasoning without becoming bureaucratic records for every change.

title: ADR-0018: Isolate Internal Documentation from Product Distribution
heading: ADR-0018: Isolate Internal Documentation from Product Distribution
text:
ADR-0018: Isolate Internal Documentation from Product Distribution
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-23

title: ADR-0018: Isolate Internal Documentation from Product Distribution
heading: Context
text:
Context
The owner requires a complete engineering knowledge system for developers and AI agents while separating it from product UI and public documentation. The existing portal uses the React/Vite application, deterministic generated references, a lazy UI import, local search, and synthetic previews. Lazy loading still emits its entire internal catalog and downloads into production artifacts. Removing navigation or adding a browser route guard would leave those files downloadable.
ADR-0008 already selects Vite and code splitting. Development-only identity behavior already uses build-time exclusion. ADR-0017 retains the portal and its sources in projects and makes composition and brand assets project-owned; it does not require shipping engineering assets in product builds. This decision complements that source-retention contract by defining distribution and publication explicitly. These mechanisms can support the requested separation without selecting another framework, authentication provider, or deployment topology.

title: ADR-0018: Isolate Internal Documentation from Product Distribution
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
Retain the full internal source catalog, generators, local `/docs` routes, search, previews, and AI-readable references. Treat the portal as a development tool. Exclude its routes, imports, UI styles, generated pages, search assets and reference downloads from every default production web build, in Orion and derived projects. Fail the product build if an accidental included import bypasses that boundary.
Allow explicit internal builds only with an operator acknowledgement that a trusted external host enforces access to the entire artifact. This build selection grants no permission and supplies no authentication. A real internal deployment requires authorization and verified host controls over assets and downloads as well as routes; API controls remain unchanged.
Product documentation belongs to the product's UI, audience, ownership and release process. Public API documentation uses a separately approved source inventory, including referenced schemas and examples. Neither public surface inherits or filters the internal catalog automatically. The foundation does not introduce a public publisher in this change.
Keep portal layout/navigation/styles inside its optional import boundary. Applications retain control of their shell, home, modules, brand and documentation presentation. Preserve the existing toolchain, repository/manifest contract, local URLs, and generated-source ownership.

title: ADR-0018: Isolate Internal Documentation from Product Distribution
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
Compile-time selection removes actual emitted bytes and reuses Vite rather than introducing an application boundary solely for packaging. Independent publication sources prevent an internal addition from becoming a public disclosure. Retaining complete generation keeps engineering discovery and agent context intact. title: API Error Contract
heading: API Error Contract
text:
API Error Contract
[Task index](../README.md) · [API principles](principles.md) · [Error handling](../architecture/error-handling.md) · [Compatibility](versioning.md)
This policy owns public failure semantics. The API's [shared error registry, envelope schema, and responder](../../apps/api/src/errors.ts) and each composed module's registered codes are canonical; the [public registry composition](../../apps/api/src/error-registry.ts) gives each code exactly one owner and rejects any duplicate, even an identical definition, and the [generated error reference](../generated/api/errors.md) lists implemented codes, messages, categories, HTTP statuses, and retry classifications. Module route contracts declare expected operation errors. Follow [ADR-0007](../adr/0007-establish-api-contract-openapi-sdk-and-configuration-schema-strategy.md) when generating OpenAPI and SDK representations.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Error Envelope

title: API Error Contract
heading: Error Code Format
text:
Error Code Format
Public codes use stable semantic `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` names. Clients branch on codes and deliberately defined structured fields, never on message text or internal exception classes. Messages are safe human explanations and may change for clarity or product localization without changing the code's meaning. Canonical repository descriptions remain English.
Infrastructure identifiers such as SQLSTATE, ORM codes, provider exceptions, filesystem paths, or runtime class names are not public semantics. Map failures to the condition consumers need to understand. Reuse an existing code for the same meaning; do not create a code for every code path, collapse materially different consumer actions into one generic code, or reuse a retired code for a new meaning.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Error Code Ownership
text:
Error Code Ownership
The feature/application owner defines business failures; the API boundary owns cross-cutting public mappings. The registry provides one canonical definition, and operation metadata refers to it. The registry enumerates stable public conditions, not every possible database/network/library exception. Do not maintain an independent manual registry in prose or generated clients.
For a new code, determine its semantic owner, expected/unexpected category, public disclosure safety, consumer action, status mapping, retry implications, optional details, and compatibility impact. Update canonical code, operation declarations, tests, and generated references together. Each module's implementation conventions explain its authorization-sensitive classification order.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Validation Errors
text:
Validation Errors
The implemented validation response is `400 VALIDATION_FAILED` with the common envelope. Do not expose validator exceptions or echo submitted values. Structural validation is distinct from a valid request that conflicts with current domain state.
Field-level problems use the envelope's optional `issues`, defined once in the [shared envelope schema](../../apps/api/src/errors.ts):
Each issue has a `path` (a JSON Pointer into the request body, never a database or ORM path) and a stable `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` `reason`.
An issue may add `fieldId`, naming a stored field that is absent from the body, and `count`, saying how many stored items cause the problem.
An issue never echoes a submitted value.
The responder keeps at most 50 issues, so an attacker-controlled payload cannot create an unbounded response. Unknown body fields still fail structural validation first.
A module sends issues only for the codes whose operations document their reasons. Today these are the catalogs module's `CATALOG_SCHEMA_INVALID`, `CATALOG_RECORD_INVALID` and `CATALOG_RECORD_REFERENCED`. Other codes, including `VALIDATION_FAILED`, carry none.
Clients branch on `code` and may use `reason` to point at the field; they must tolerate unknown reasons. Adding a reason is additive; changing a reason's meaning follows [compatibility review](versioning.md).

title: API Error Contract
heading: Mapping and disclosure
text:
Mapping and disclosure
HTTP status conveys broad protocol meaning; public codes convey application semantics. The [generated registry](../generated/api/errors.md) is the current status mapping. Validation uses `400`, authentication `401`, permission denial `403`, absent/hidden resources `404`, state/version conflicts `409`, rate limiting `429`, unexpected failures `500`, and service unavailability `503` where declared.
Authentication and authorization failures follow their [security policies](../security/authentication.md). Avoid account enumeration and disclosure of hidden resource existence, cross-tenant data, claims, or policy internals. An absent and inaccessible resource may deliberately share `404`; test that behavior.
Expected domain conflicts, stale versions, and incompatible idempotency-key reuse are explicit outcomes. Distinguish safe replay from a conflicting new intent. They should not become internal incidents simply because code represents them as exceptions.
Translate known database constraints at the persistence/application boundary according to business meaning. Unexpected database failures stay unexpected; do not disguise every exception as invalid user input.
Translate provider business rejection separately from dependency unavailability, configuration failure, or unknown outcome. Expose vendor-specific distinctions only when consumers need them, never raw provider content.
Use a safe generic error for unexpected failures. Never serialize arbitrary exceptions, stack traces, SQL, secret values, internal paths/hostnames, or diagnostic dumps. Do not return ordinary API failures as hidden error objects inside `200` responses.
Public status is not internal severity: expected denials may matter to security monitoring, and a transient dependency failure may be operationally serious. [Error reporting](../reliability/error-reporting.md) owns that distinction.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Unknown Outcome
text:
Unknown Outcome
A timeout, disconnect, or commit error may leave the caller uncertain whether a write or external effect occurred. Retryability cannot be inferred from HTTP status or transient infrastructure failure alone. Define whether the operation is known not to have occurred, safely replayable, or requires state reconciliation. Introduce a distinct public unknown-outcome code only when consumers need different handling.
A public retry hint, if introduced, must be machine-readable, bounded, and accurate for the operation. Rate-limit guidance must not disclose anti-abuse internals. Never imply a non-idempotent write is safe to repeat merely because the registry classifies a failure as transient. Each module's recovery conventions own its create replay and mutation reconciliation behavior.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Details and additional delivery modes
text:
Details and additional delivery modes
Every public details object needs a typed schema and a consumer purpose. Include only information safe for that caller; omit record dumps, protected resource/tenant identifiers, authorization evaluation, credentials, and provider payloads. Cross-cutting correlation/retry metadata should remain distinguishable from domain details. Once consumed, field meaning and shape are compatibility-sensitive.
When additional modes are introduced:
Mode
Error requirement
Webhook or upload
Follow the operation/provider contract while minimizing signature-validation or scanning details. Bound and classify upload failures explicitly.
Asynchronous work
A successful acceptance response does not guarantee eventual success. Externally visible job status maps worker failures to stable public semantics, never worker exceptions.
Batch/partial success
Define atomic versus partial processing and item identity in an operation-specific result. Do not ambiguously overload the ordinary single-error envelope.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Diagnostics and consumer behavior
text:
Diagnostics and consumer behavior
Report an unexpected occurrence once at its authoritative boundary. Preserve useful internal causal evidence only within [redaction rules](../security/telemetry-redaction.md); preservation never authorizes raw exception-message or stack export. The current runtime records allowlisted diagnostic fields rather than arbitrary error content. Expected validation, business, and access failures may contribute to safe metrics/security/audit signals without becoming unexpected incidents.
Clients and SDKs must preserve structured error semantics and correlation, and provide a safe fallback for unknown codes. Application consumers should not depend on framework-specific transport exceptions for business meaning. Product code decides whether to display safe server copy or localized client text; it must not parse that copy. The current thin SDK exposes generated response/error typing without adding a separate error-class hierarchy.
Code meaning, status mappings, details, categories where consumed, and retry behavior require [compatibility review](versioning.md). Adding a code can break exhaustive consumers; renaming/removing a code or changing meaning is potentially breaking. Optional details are only additive if actual clients tolerate them.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Change and verification checklist
text:
Change and verification checklist
Inspect the registry, similar conditions, owning operation, actual consumers, authorization/disclosure policy, and compatibility commitments.
Define the safe semantic mapping and outcome/retry behavior. Add details only when needed, with explicit schema and size limits.
Verify the real transport envelope, status, code, safe message, correlation, hidden-resource handling, and relevant failure paths. Test absent/invalid/expired credentials and other lifecycle states only where that mechanism exists.
Inject unexpected failures and assert that secrets, SQL, provider data, input values, stacks, and internal paths do not escape. Verify one appropriate diagnostic event and safe retry metadata if present.
Regenerate and check the registry/OpenAPI/SDK references through [validation](../validation.md). Preserve current checks for registered unique codes, operation declarations, and freshness; extend checks for any new detail schemas or released compatibility obligations.

title: API Principles
heading: Ownership and transport boundaries
text:
Ownership and transport boundaries
An API exposes an owned application capability, not an arbitrary database table. Each operation needs a clear domain owner, consumer, and canonical contract. Resources and explicit commands are both appropriate when they express real behavior; do not generate CRUD or generic updates for every persisted entity.
Transport adapters own routing, request validation, authentication integration, safe request context, protocol/error mapping, and response serialization. Application operations and domain rules should not depend on HTTP objects, headers, status codes, or framework APIs unless the behavior itself is transport-specific. Pass only the trusted context an operation needs.
Persistence records, domain entities, API payloads, events, and UI models have distinct responsibilities. Reuse a representation only when its semantics genuinely match. Explicitly map allowed inputs and outputs: never pass an untrusted body directly to persistence or serialize internal objects merely because they are available. This prevents mass assignment and accidental disclosure while allowing internal refactoring without consumer breakage.

title: API Principles
heading: Canonical API Contract
text:
Canonical API Contract
Maintain wire-oriented TypeBox schemas and route metadata as the authored source. Fastify uses them for validation and serialization; generated OpenAPI 3.1 describes the interoperable boundary; `openapi-typescript` and `openapi-fetch` provide the default typed client. Every exposed operation must have a stable, unique `operationId`.
Define request/response shapes, constraints, authentication, expected errors, and non-structural semantics deliberately before exposing behavior. Do not separately maintain equivalent runtime validators, TypeScript interfaces, OpenAPI schemas, SDK types, or reference tables. Generated artifacts are reproducible representations and must not be hand-edited. Ordinary internal types need not become TypeBox schemas.
The API owns its contracts. Extract a shared contract package only for genuine shared ownership. Such a package must not depend on persistence, backend framework implementation, server secrets, or UI code. First-party consumers use the generated SDK and must not import server implementations or database types. The SDK may provide transport, types, credential hooks, and error decoding; it must not own backend business authorization or persistence. Successful-response runtime revalidation is not automatic; introduce it only for a demonstrated trust or reliability requirement.

title: API Principles
heading: Validation
text:
Validation
Treat bodies, query/path parameters, headers, cookies, uploads, webhooks, and client identifiers as untrusted. Validate structural input at the trusted boundary before application logic relies on it. Structural validation, domain validity, authentication, and authorization remain separate checks.
For each field, define meaning, required/optional status, omission versus explicit `null`, type, format, bounds, allowed values, classification, and exposure. Normalize only when domain semantics require it; do not silently modify user content for convenience. Unknown-field behavior must be deliberate and compatible with the consumer contract. Separate create, replacement, partial-update, summary, detail, and privileged schemas where their semantics differ instead of building one universally optional model.
Use meaningful text and numeric limits based on product needs and resource cost. Bounded states should use explicit enums; consider extensibility under [versioning](versioning.md). Distinguish instants, calendar dates, local times, time zones, and durations. Money requires currency, units, and precision; exact financial amounts must not rely on ambiguous floating-point representations. Use clear English names and canonical descriptions, positive boolean semantics where practical, and established domain terminology. Product localization does not change machine identifiers.

title: API Principles
heading: Identifiers
text:
Identifiers
Public identifiers represent stable resource identity. They may coincide with storage keys when that is an intentional contract, but must not expose sensitive structure or grant authority. Treat opaque identifiers as opaque. Client-generated IDs are allowed only when explicitly designed for an actual offline, distributed, or idempotency need. Changing storage must not accidentally change public identity.

title: API Principles
heading: Authentication
text:
Authentication
Protected operations derive identity and capabilities from the [trusted authentication boundary](../security/authentication.md) and enforce [authorization](../security/authorization.md) on the server. Caller-supplied roles, owner IDs, permissions, tenant IDs, feature flags, or UI visibility cannot grant access. A tenant path alone does not establish membership. Public operations must be explicitly public; administrative/debug capabilities require deliberate privilege, output, and environment controls.
Make operation security requirements discoverable. Apply stronger controls where credentials, personal data, finances, or administration require them. Hidden resources may deliberately share not-found semantics with absent resources; preserve and test the disclosure policy. Keep bearer credentials out of URLs except for an explicitly designed protocol requiring a short-lived capability. Gateway authentication never replaces application authorization.
